sections.cite: Dr. Patricia Langford, MD, Board-Certified Gastroenterologist

paragraphs: I need to be honest with you about something that’s been keeping me up at night.
In 22 years of practicing gastroenterology — seeing patients with Crohn’s, colitis, IBS, diverticulitis — I thought I’d seen every kind of digestive dysfunction there is.
Then GLP-1 medications exploded. Ozempic. Wegovy. Mounjaro. Zepbound.
And suddenly, my waiting room filled with a new kind of patient.

Women in their 50s, 60s, 70s. Educated. Put-together. Losing weight beautifully. Scale going down every week. Clothes fitting again for the first time in decades. Compliments coming from every direction.
But privately? They were falling apart.
Five days without a bowel movement. Seven days. Eleven days.
Bloating so severe they looked six months pregnant — which defeats the entire purpose of losing weight.
Sulfur burps so foul they were terrified to open their mouths in meetings, in cars, at dinner with their husbands.
And every single one of them said the same thing:

sections.text: “I’ve tried EVERYTHING. Miralax. Dulcolax. Fiber. Magnesium. Enemas. Smooth Move tea. Nothing works.”

paragraphs: And they were right. Nothing they tried could work.
Because every single product they were taking was designed to work on the colon — the very end of the digestive tract.
But the problem wasn’t in their colon.
The problem was something I’d never seen at this scale before. Something forming in their stomachs. Something I now call:

sections.text: “Stomach Ink” — The Hidden Reason Nothing You’ve Tried Has Worked

paragraphs: Let me explain what’s actually happening inside your body right now — because your doctor almost certainly hasn’t.
When you take Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, or any GLP-1 medication, it works by slowing your stomach’s emptying rate by up to 70%.
That’s the entire mechanism. Slow stomach = feel full = eat less = lose weight.
And it works. Brilliantly.
But here’s what the prescribing information glosses over in one line of fine print:
When food sits in your stomach 2-3 times longer than normal, it doesn’t just “wait there.”
Your digestive acids keep working on it. Bacteria begin fermenting it. Proteins break down and release hydrogen sulfide gas — that’s the rotten-egg sulfur burps.
And the mixture itself? It thickens. Darkens. Becomes viscous.
It turns into a thick, dark, ink-like sludge that your now-weakened stomach muscles simply cannot push forward.

“Think of it this way: your stomach is a muscular bag that’s supposed to churn food and push it into your small intestine every 4-5 hours. GLP-1 medications tell those muscles to slow to a crawl. So the food sits. Ferments. Hardens. After 12, 18, 24 hours, what was once a normal meal has become something closer to wet concrete. I call it ‘Stomach Ink’ — because that’s what it looks like on endoscopy. Dark, thick, and stuck.”
And here’s the part that explains everything you’ve been through:

sections.text: Why Miralax, Dulcolax, Fiber, Enemas — Everything in Your Medicine Cabinet — Can Never Fix This

paragraphs: Look at every remedy you’ve tried. Every single one:

Dulcolax — stimulant laxative. Forces colon muscles to contract.
Fiber supplements — adds bulk to stool in the colon.

paragraphs: Do you see the pattern?

sections.text: Every single remedy targets the COLON — the last 5 feet of your digestive tract. But the Stomach Ink is sitting in your STOMACH — the first organ in the chain. You’re trying to unclog a backed-up sink by mopping the floor.

paragraphs: The colon is the end of digestion. Your problem is at the beginning.

The Stomach Ink has to move out of your stomach first. Until it does, nothing downstream matters. You can take every laxative on the pharmacy shelf — the ink sits there, fermenting, producing gas, hardening further, while you suffer.
This is why you can drink an entire bottle of Miralax over a weekend and nothing happens.
This is why you’ve sat on the toilet for twenty minutes, pushing, and gotten nothing but rabbit pellets.
This is why the food you ate Tuesday is still sitting there Thursday — and you can taste it when you burp.
It was never about your colon. It was always about the ink.

sections.text: So What Actually Dissolves “Stomach Ink”?

paragraphs: Once I understood what was happening, the question became obvious: how do you get the stomach moving again?
Not the colon. The stomach.
The answer, it turns out, has been hiding in a vegetable that millions of women were already juicing — without knowing exactly why it helped.
Celery.

Now, before you roll your eyes — I’m not talking about the TikTok celery juice trend. I’m talking about a specific compound inside celery called apigenin that has a very specific pharmacological effect:

“Apigenin is a natural prokinetic. That means it gently stimulates the smooth muscle contractions of the stomach wall — the exact contractions that GLP-1 medications suppress. Think of it as physical therapy for a paralyzed gut. You’re not forcing anything. You’re waking up the muscles so they can do what they’re designed to do: push food forward.”
This is fundamentally different from every laxative on the market.
Laxatives force the colon to purge. Prokinetics wake up the stomach so it can push.
One is downstream brute force. The other is upstream rehabilitation.
And here’s what gets me the most frustrated as a clinician:

The research on apigenin and gastric motility has existed for years. We’ve known that natural prokinetic compounds can support stomach emptying. But there was never a product designed specifically for GLP-1 users — because the pharmaceutical industry makes more money selling you Linzess at $600/month or Zofran at $15 a pill than telling you about a compound from celery.
